Aberdeen boss Mario Frick's heavy metal football is music to the ears of their long-suffering supporters

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1266 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dailymail

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • By CALUM CROWE, SCOTTISH DEPUTY CHIEF SPORTS WRITER.
  • Published: 16:57 EST, 23 November 2026 | Updated: 16:57 EST, 23 November 2026.
  • As they embarked on the long journey home from Kilmarnock on Saturday night, Aberdeen supporters would surely have felt a little extra spring in their step.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

By CALUM CROWE, SCOTTISH DEPUTY CHIEF SPORTS WRITER.

Published: 16:57 EST, 23 November 2026 | Updated: 16:57 EST, 23 November 2026.

As they embarked on the long journey home from Kilmarnock on Saturday night, Aberdeen supporters would surely have felt a little extra spring in their step.

If 2026 felt like it had been shaping up to be something of an annus horribilis, a 4-2 victory at Rugby Park undoubtedly lifted some of the gloom that had been hanging over the club these past few months.

Granted, a sample size of only one match under Mario Frick is very small. Nobody would be of a mind to get carried away with themselves just yet, especially given that Killie are easily the worst team in the league.

But there was enough in the performance, particularly during a first half which saw them score three goals in 30 minutes, to suggest that a brighter future could lie ahead under the upcoming manager.

In a recent development, aberdeen were aggressive, they played on the front foot, and they attacked with pace. Most of all, they were actually exciting and entertaining to watch.

Those were boxes they never ticked at any point during Stephen Robinson's time in charge. Robinson failed at Aberdeen and his team were routinely awful in terms of the quality of football they served up.

Mario Frick celebrates after a 4-2 win over Kilmarnock in his first game as Aberdeen manager.

Ante Palaversa is back in the Aberdeen team after becoming the forgotten man of Pittodrie.

Aberdeen striker Kevin Nisbet rediscovered the feelgood factor by scoring twice at Rugby Park.

In the space of only 90 minutes, Frick did more to send a wave of positivity through supporters than Robinson ever managed to do in his eight months at the helm.

The shift in mood has been as profound as it has been instantaneous, with Frick's so-called heavy metal football music to the fans' ears.

Headlines of Super Mario were always likely to follow, but Frick and his players will face an altogether tougher examination when they take on Rangers at Ibrox tomorrow.

It is an intriguing contest on various levels, with Rangers unbeaten in 13 matches as Derek McInnes goes up against his former club once again.

Given that these teams met in the Premier Sports Cup only a few weeks ago, perhaps the greatest barometer of Frick's impact will be whether Aberdeen can pose more of a threat than they did at Hampden.

It has been revealed that but what has changed? After such a turgid run of form that left players looking completely bereft of any confidence and cohesion, how was Frick able to generate an immediate improvement?

Speaking after the win at Killie, Frick was asked what sort of message he had given to the players given that time together on the training pitch had been fairly limited.

According to recent reports, 'I told them they should play like they did when they were young. In those days they didn't think about mistakes.

'They didn't think about anything negative. They played only to win, for fun.'.

Sources indicate that it was simple but refreshing. In an age of increasingly complex coaching jargon, Frick's message was intended to liberate his players – and it worked a treat.

Industry observers note that aberdeen went 2-0 up inside 12 minutes, with Kevin Nisbet scoring twice. The team looked free from the trauma of the Robinson era.

Even when Kilmarnock fought back and the game became more chaotic, Aberdeen retained enough attacking threat and collective belief to close it out.

It has been revealed that it was a huge result. A defeat would have dropped Aberdeen to the foot of the table. Instead, they climbed five places and, more importantly, rediscovered a feelgood factor.

In his previous utterances, Frick was clear that goalscoring has been the central problem.

Industry observers note that his previous teams at Vaduz and Luzern were known for their attacking output. At Luzern last season they scored 76 goals.

According to recent reports, aberdeen had managed only 12 in 12 league matches before his arrival. The early evidence suggests the players have absorbed the message rapidly.

Frick's insistence on the basics – aggression, willingness to work, positive body language – appears to have cut through more effectively than more elaborate instructions might have done.

Recent findings suggest that this is consistent with the picture painted by those who worked with him in Switzerland. Frick is not a rigid systems coach wedded to a single formation.

It has been revealed that he has most often used a 4-4-2 diamond, but the shape is secondary to the mentality. High pressing to force turnovers, rapid counter-attacks, and a sense of freedom imbued to his players.

Sources indicate that all of which makes tomorrow's clash at Ibrox all the more compelling. Aberdeen have lost their last eight meetings with Rangers in all competitions.

The previous two encounters this season, one in the Premiership and one in the Premier Sports Cup, were both settled by late Rangers goals.

It has been revealed that the contrast in styles will be stark. Rangers are likely to control territory and force Aberdeen to defend for longer periods than they did at Rugby Park.

Frick's side will need to show that the freedom he has granted them does not dissolve into naivety when the opponent is stronger and more experienced.

The high press that worked so effectively against a struggling Killie side will have to be timed with greater precision.

The attacking play will require clinical decision-making in the final third. And the defensive structure, which Frick identified as the main area for improvement after Saturday, will be examined under more sustained pressure.

It has been revealed that frick has already spoken of aiming higher than mere survival. In a league which is always extremely tight in the mid-table, top six should be the minimum target.

That may have sounded optimistic a fortnight ago. But the win at Kilmarnock suggested Aberdeen have enough about themselves to be looking up rather than over their shoulders.

The squad still needs greater consistency and, in certain areas, greater quality.

But there is already evidence to suggest he can get a tune out of some players who either under-performed under Robinson or, in some cases, those who had been totally discarded.

Ante Palaversa would surely be chief among them. The Croatian midfielder hardly kicked a ball under Robinson and had become the forgotten man at Pittodrie.

Brought in to make his first league start of the season, his performance at Killie and the way he controlled things in midfield made his exclusion under Robinson look all the more bizarre.

None of this is to say that Aberdeen are suddenly a top-class football team. At best, they remain very much a work in progress.

Yet, crucially, Frick immediately has the supporters onboard in a way that Robinson never managed to do.

Frick and his players could yet be given a major reality check if they were to suffer a hefty defeat to a Rangers side unbeaten in 13 matches.

But there is belief and positivity in the camp at Pittodrie. Feelgood factors in football can often be fragile and often short-lived, but they are also real.

When players begin to play with freedom and confidence, results usually tend to take care of themselves.

Recent findings suggest that frick has not yet transformed Aberdeen. He has, however, given the players and the fans a reason to believe that a brighter future could lie ahead.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Liverpool are reportedly among a number of clubs interested in signing Borussia Monchengladbach wonderkid Wael Mohya.
  • Earlier this month, the 17-year-old attacker earned his first-ever senior international call-up to Jurgen Klopp’s Germany squad after making a notable impression as a first-team regular at club level.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

By Oliver Thomas | 24 Nov 2026 12:22.

Liverpool are reportedly among a number of clubs interested in signing Borussia Monchengladbach wonderkid Wael Mohya.

Earlier this month, the 17-year-old attacker earned his first-ever senior international call-up to Jurgen Klopp’s Germany squad after making a notable impression as a first-team regular at club level.

Mohya broke into Monchengladbach’s senior side midway through last season and became the club’s youngest-ever goalscorer against Bayern Munich in March of this year.

He has since developed into an increasingly influential player under head coach Alexander Blessin this term, featuring in all 10 Bundesliga matches as well as two DFB-Pokal games.

Mohya became the fourth youngest-player in Bundesliga history to score in consecutive games in October, contributing with a goal and an assist in a standout display in a 3-2 win against Stuttgart.

The dynamic and versatile attacker, who is comfortable operating centrally or out wide, has produced several impressive performances that have subsequently caught the eye of some of Europe’s biggest clubs.

According to TEAMtalk, Andoni Iraola’s Liverpool have shown concrete interest in Mohya and have intensively scouted the teenager.

The report adds the Reds are ‘ready to battle’ with high-flying Brighton & Hove Albion, who presently sit second in the Premier League table and have also been closely monitoring the attacker.

Bundesliga giants Bayern Munich, Borussia Dortmund, Bayer Leverkusen and RB Leipzig are also said to be keeping an eye on Mohya’s progress, while Real Madrid, Barcelona and AC Milan are some of the big clubs abroad who have recently entered the race for his signature.

As things stand, Monchengladbach are yet to receive any formal offers for Mohya or enter negotiations with another club despite growing interest in his services.

Mohya’s contract is due to expire in June 2028, and Monchengladbach sporting director Rouven Schroder recently insisted that “he is definitely not for sale in January,” adding: “The rest will depend on how the market develops.”.

The youngster is viewed as a key part of Monchengladbach’s intends for this season, and it is understood that an offer in the region of €45m (£37.7m) is what it would take to persuade the German club to open talks over a possible sale in the coming transfer windows.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Torreense welcome Celtic to Estadio Municipal de Leiria on Thursday night for a matchday five clash in the league phase of the Europa League.
  • The hosts are 19th in the standings with six points from four games, while the visitors are 32nd with three points after four matches.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

By Ellis Stevens | 24 Nov 2026 12:23.

Torreense welcome Celtic to Estadio Municipal de Leiria on Thursday night for a matchday five clash in the league phase of the Europa League.

The hosts are 19th in the standings with six points from four games, while the visitors are 32nd with three points after four matches.

Torreense made history by defeating Sporting Lisbon 2-1 in the Taca de Portugal final last season, marking the club's first major trophy and securing their qualification to the Europa League.

Torreense, as a result, became the first non-top flight club to qualify for the revamped league phase of the competition, and Azul-grenas have performed admirably in their opening four fixtures.

Thursday's hosts have secured two wins and suffered two defeats in their first four games, leaving Torreense placed 19th in the league phase table and on course to qualify for the knockouts.

The latest of those victories, a dramatic 3-2 win against Ararat-Armenia that featured two goals in stoppage time to come from 2-1 down to secure the win, came under upcoming boss Joao Nuno, who was appointed after Luis Miguel Valado Tralhao mutually agreed to step down as manager.

Nuno recorded one win and one draw in his first two games, but the manager has since suffered back-to-back defeats heading into this match, leaving Torreense eager to avoid enduring a third consecutive loss.

Torreense will draw confidence from their impressive displays in the Europa League, while visitors Celtic have shown signs of weakness in this competition this term.

The Bhoys have won only one of their four league phase fixtures, alongside three defeats, scoring just six goals and conceding a considerable 11 goals in that time.

Martin O'Neill's side actually lost each of their first three league phase fixtures, results that coincided with a miserable run across all competitions, during which they recorded six defeats, one draw and just three wins between mid-September and the beginning of November.

However, a 3-2 triumph over Besiktas on matchday four of the league phase, featuring an 87th-minute winner from Camilo Duran, has sparked a three-game winning run, subsequently defeating both Kilmarnock (1-0) and St Mirren (4-1).

Celtic will be looking to extend that winning streak and secure just their second win of the league phase on Thursday, with the Bhoys hoping to move closer to the qualification places.

While Celtic have returned to winning ways in recent matches, concerns remain about their form on the road, having lost three of their last five away fixtures across all competitions.

Torreense form (all competitions):.

Celtic form (all competitions):.

Torreense will be without Jorge Aguirre for Thursday's fixture after the forward was sent off in the matchday four clash with Ararat-Armenia, and Adama Baradji is also not expected to feature due to an injury concern.

In Aguirre's absence, Musa Drammeh, who scored in the defeat to Benfica last time out, should lead the line, with Carlos Reina providing support in attacking midfield.

Meanwhile, Duran, who has scored 14 goals in 22 appearances for Celtic this season, should lead the line, with Sebastian Tounekti, Benjamin Nygren and Haissem Hassan providing attacking support.

Further back, Alex Oxlade-Chamberlain and Callum McGregor could feature at the base of midfield, with Cameron Carter-Vickers and Liam Scales in central defence.

Torreense possible starting lineup:.

Olmeta; Mutombo, Diadie, Volnei, Vazquez; Marques, Alfaro; Guerrero, Reina, Jean; Drammeh.

Celtic possible starting lineup:.

Johnstone; Lotomba, Carter-Vickers, Scales, Tierney; McGregor, Oxlade-Chamberlain; Hassan, Nygren, Tounekti; Duran.

Although Celtic have struggled on the road in recent matches and shown signs of weakness in the Europa League, the away side should have the quality to overcome their second-division hosts and secure the win.

Adrien Rabiot has had an outstanding start to the 2026-27 season, and he is showing absolutely no signs of slowing down.

La Gazzetta dello Sport (seen below) begin a report this morning by pointing out what Rabiot remarked after Milan’s 5-1 demolition of Frosinone on Sunday: “An assist is better than a goal.” He was the man of the match against Frosinone: five goals were scored, yet none bore his name.

Still, the Frenchman made himself the stand-out performer, thanks to his tireless running, leadership, and a series of decisive passes, not to mention his role in the opening goal, which came via an own-goal.

Recent findings suggest that it was a summer of doubts for Rabiot, given that his extended vacation was interpreted by some as a sign of discontent and a longing to reunite with his former mentor – Massimiliano Allegri – at Napoli. Yet, he has transformed into a cornerstone of this new era.

Recent findings suggest that the former PSG man is now a decisive force on the pitch, integral to Ruben Amorim’s tactical framework, and a true leader. The numbers demonstrate this perfectly: Rabiot is the first midfielder to contribute to at least one goal (scoring or assisting) in seven consecutive Serie A appearances since Kaká in 2004.

With five goals and six assists, he recently became the first midfielder in the last 20 years of Serie A to record more than 10 goal contributions within the first 10 matches of a single season. In total, Rabiot has surpassed the milestone of 50 direct goal involvements in Serie A (29 goals and 22 assists).

Industry observers note that milan trust him, and the feeling is mutual. As previously mentioned, the very fact that he remained with the Rossoneri over the summer – publicly reaffirming his commitment to the club – is reflected in his attitude, both on and off the field.

Sources indicate that he is always smiling and highly active on social media; his numbers on Instagram are as impressive as his stats on the field. He posts photos of his goals, his celebrations and embraces with Diego Moreira, with whom he is clearly building a close bond.

Amorim said after the game: “Adrien can play as a ’10,’ an attacking midfielder, an ‘8,’ or even as a playmaker – though he doesn’t particularly like that role. He is certainly one of the best players I have ever coached, and one of the best midfielders in Europe.”.

Speaking to Telefoot, Rabiot addressed the topic of his excellent start statistically: “It’s a positive thing to have players capable of being decisive, even if they aren’t forwards. It also serves as an encouragement to those around us.

“At Milan, we have quite a few young players, and it’s important for them to have role models in their day-to-day lives. I had only been back from vacation for a week when he was already talking to me about a contract renewal.

In a recent development, “I told him, ‘Coach, take it easy!’ (laughs). But, naturally, it’s significant for a player to feel that kind of trust—the coach relies on us, holds us in high regard, and makes us feel important.”.

Further significant remarks regarding Rabiot were made by Gerry Cardinale on the eve of the most recent league match, specifically concerning his imminent contract renewal.

“I love Adrien, he’s one of my favourite players. He’s fantastic. I have enormous respect for him and his family. We are in talks, and I hope we reach a happy conclusion soon. I believe he should be a signature player for Milan. Could it be a Christmas gift for the fans? Absolutely, and for me, too.”.

Recent findings suggest that the renewal will happen, and it will happen soon. Any delay until the latest year should not be interpreted as a negative sign. Rather, it reflects the fact that everything is already settled, and there is no rush to finalise the signature.

In a recent development, adrien’s current deal – which runs until 2028 – will be extended to 2030, with an additional one-year option. From his current age of 31, he will remain a fixture in the Rossoneri midfield until he is 33 or 34, the prime of his footballing maturity.

Now into his thirties, he will also earn a more lucrative contract than his current one, which pays him €3.5m net per season. It is worth noting that in the summer of 2025, Adrien was acquired from Marseille for €7m after a training-ground altercation with Jonathan Rowe.

It was, by any definition, a fantastic deal. As for the future, Rabiot has a role model he can observe from very close quarters: “Modrić trains as if he were 21, he’s an example to follow. The closer you get to the end of your career, the more you start to savor every moment. I try to do the same.”.

With the imminent contract extension, Adrien Rabiot is also set to conclude his career in the red and black colours, and that would make everyone happy.

Published: 16:30 EST, 23 November 2026 | Updated: 17:03 EST, 23 November 2026.

Mauricio Pochettino will have less than £50million to buy Manchester United out of trouble in the January transfer window.

Pochettino admitted that United are in a relegation battle after a painful 4-0 defeat to Liverpool in his first game in charge left the club second from bottom of the Premier League.

It’s understood the Argentine will have a limited budget well under £50million with United’s hands tied by the league’s new financial rules. Pochettino is only expected to make two new signings in January, even if one of them is a loan deal.

Sources have not ruled out the possibility of United gambling if there is a genuine threat of the club being relegated for the first time in 53 years, but they would still have to spend responsibly.

The defeat to Liverpool underlined the need for Pochettino to strengthen in central defence, with Brentford’s Nathan Collins emerging as a strong candidate ahead of Calvin Bassey, who is expected to sign a newly introduced contract with Fulham, and Everton’s Jarrad Branthwaite who is valued at over £70million.

United also want a left-back after failing to sign cover for Luke Shaw in the summer when they were linked with Barcelona’s Alejandro Balde and Rayan Ait-Nouri of Manchester City. Both those players could be potential targets again.

Mauricio Pochettino will have less than £50million to try and fix Manchester United in January.

Pochettino is only expected to make two new signings in January - pictured: Chief executive Omar Berrada (left) and director of football Jason Wilcox (centre).

Pochettino would also like a new striker after Benjamin Sesko’s shin injury left him short of firepower until the New Year.

Monaco’s Folarin Balogun, who played under Pochettino for the US national team, Leeds striker Dominic Calvert-Lewin and Ivan Toney, the former Brentford centre-forward now playing for Al-Ahli, have all been linked with a move to Old Trafford.

However, Toney’s £500,000-a-week wages put him out of United’s reach, and Leeds are keen to extend Calvert-Lewin’s contract which is worth £180,000-a-week.

Meanwhile, United are appealing to the FA over Leny Yoro’s controversial red card against Liverpool.

Yoro was sent off in the eighth minute at Anfield for a challenge on Alexander Isak on the edge of the penalty box. The Frenchman was dismissed by referee Sam Barrott, and Dominik Szoboszlai scored Liverpool’s first goal from the free-kick.

However, United insist that Yoro did not deny Isak a clear goalscoring opportunity because goalkeeper Senne Lammens would have reached the ball first.

The club have notified the FA of their intention to appeal in the hope of having Yoro’s one-match ban overturned so he can play against Brentford at Old Trafford on Saturday.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Chelsea defender Wesley Fofana has admitted that he seriously considered retiring from football during Enzo Maresca’s time in charge at Stamford Bridge.
  • The one-cap France international joined the West Londoners from Leicester City for a reported £75m in the summer of 2022 and has since played 81 times for the club across all competitions.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

By Oliver Thomas | 24 Nov 2026 12:42.

Chelsea defender Wesley Fofana has admitted that he seriously considered retiring from football during Enzo Maresca’s time in charge at Stamford Bridge.

The one-cap France international joined the West Londoners from Leicester City for a reported £75m in the summer of 2022 and has since played 81 times for the club across all competitions.

Fofana’s career at Chelsea has largely been disrupted by injury, missing a total of 41 matches during Maresca’s 18-month reign with the Blues.

While Fofana began the 2024-25 season fit after recovering from a year-long ACL tear, two major hamstring injuries wiped out nearly six months of his campaign.

The 25-year-old centre-back has since opened up about how the psychological strain that came with a rash of injuries almost led to the decision to prematurely call time on his career.

Speaking in an interview for Zack Nani TV, as quoted by the Evening Standard, Fofana said: “There was a period when I was recovering from my cruciate ligament and meniscus injuries.

“Then I suffered two consecutive hamstring strains under Enzo Maresca, when I really decided: ‘That’s it, I’m retiring, I’m done playing.’ I was serious.

“I really wanted to stop, because, for the first time in my life, I wasn’t happy anymore. It wasn’t just about being injured or not playing; my whole life was completely shattered. I wasn’t myself anymore. I sincerely believed that, in the future, I would only get injured.

Industry observers note that “I thought to myself: ‘That’s it, football isn’t for me, I’m too fragile.’ I even used Abou Diaby as an example. I thought to myself: ’I guess I’m the Abou Diaby of our generation. There has to be someone like that, and it happened to me. It’s my destiny, I accept it.’”.

According to recent reports, fofana added: “Of course, I was very sad and didn’t want to stop, because I was living my dream. At that point, I called my agents so we could sit down and talk, telling them, ‘Okay, I’ve decided to retire.’.

“They started analysing the situation with me, talking about contracts and all that: ‘It’s simple, you still have several years left on your contract, and there’s a lot of money to be made.

“Even if you really decide to stop playing, you still have to come every day, keep smiling, and even if you’re injured, you have to honour your contract for your future.’.

It has been revealed that “But at that moment, I really felt that the pain football caused me far outweighed the joy, so why continue? I was in pain almost 100 per cent of the time.

“Every time I gritted my teeth, played a few games, and just started to find a little love and joy in life again, bang, I’d get injured again.”.

Fofana has since made positive progress in building up his strength and fitness; he played 38 times for Chelsea in all competitions last season and has started seven of the first 11 Premier League matches under latest manager Xabi Alonso so far this term.

Last month, Alonso publicly backed Fofana as an "crucial," "focused," and "mature" first-team figure, who is under contract at Stamford Bridge until the summer of 2029.

When Jurgen Klopp declared his departure from Liverpool in January 2024 many supporters worried what the future might look like at Anfield.

Concerns were initially unfounded, with the Reds lifting the Premier League title in their very first season post-Klopp, but things have become complicated since then.

Arne Slot, the man who delivered the club's 20th league title, was relieved of his duties over the summer after a disappointing fifth place finish and Andoni Iraola was appointed as his replacement.

The Spaniard has enjoyed a steady start to life in L4, and the Reds are looking more like the team Klopp left behind with every week that passes.

Iraola is the next KloppLiverpool's dominating victory over Manchester United on Sunday was Iraola's biggest result since taking the reins in Merseyside. The win saw the Reds move just one point behind second place Brighton and seven points off league leaders Arsenal. A title challenge is still a bit optimistic, but the team are certainly starting to close the gap to the league's best.

Liverpool's dominating victory over Manchester United on Sunday was Iraola's biggest result since taking the reins in Merseyside.

The win saw the Reds move just one point behind second place Brighton and seven points off league leaders Arsenal.

A title challenge is still a bit optimistic, but the team are certainly starting to close the gap to the league's best.

Iraola's win over the Red Devils saw him set a record only better by Klopp himself, with the Spaniard now unbeaten in seven Premier League matches against United.

7 - Andoni Iraola is unbeaten in his seven Premier League matches against Manchester United (W3 D4). The only manager to record a longer unbeaten run against them in the competition is Jürgen Klopp (8 - 2018-2022). Intensity. https://t.co/uRN2OfkdF4.

The only manager to go on a longer run was Klopp, who was unbeaten against his bitter rivals for eight consecutive league games between 2018 and 2022.

Of course, it is too early to say that Iraola's tenure will be as successful as Klopp's, but early signs are positive and the 44-year-old has managed to get more out of many of his players than Slot did.

Some kinks in the midfield still need to be ironed out, but overall the team are starting to consistently deliver at a level that the Anfield faithful have become accustomed to over the past decade.

Supporters will be hopeful that Iraola can continue to mirror Klopp, and that he can bring as much success to Anfield as the legendary German boss did.

💡 Key Takeaways

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

For Star Trek fans, he was the legendary Captain Picard; the British actor and director Patrick Stewart, longtime member of the  Royal Shakespeare Company, died on Thursday at the age of 86 following a "brief and poignant journey" with Alzheimer's disease and Lewy body dementia, according to an official statement on his social media accounts.

In Los Angeles, California, far away from the small English village of Mirfield where he was born, Stewart achieved world fame. He was 47 years old when he landed the role of a lifetime in the legendary science fiction series Star Trek: Playing Captain Jean-Luc Picard in "Star Trek: The Next Generation," he stepped into the shoes of the legendary Captain James T. Kirk, played by William Shatner.

Stewart brought a calm, measured and distinctly British presence that promptly made Picard a fan favorite and a cult figure in the Star Trek universe. He returned to the role decades later in the spin-off series "Star Trek: Picard," which ended in 2023, proving the character's enduring appeal.

It has been revealed that as Captain Jean-Luc Picard, he led the crew of the starship Enterprise, a spaceship with the sizeable mission: "To explore strange upcoming worlds. To seek out new life and new civilizations" — and most importantly, "to boldly go where no man has gone before!".

In a recent development, stewart's interest in acting was sparked in the early 1950s when a teacher asked him to recite a work by Shakespeare. His passion for Shakespeare stayed with him until the end.

According to recent reports, his parents were far removed from the glamor of the theatrical world. His father was a highly respected officer in the British Army during World War II, but at home, he was an abusive husband, and young Patrick had to helplessly witness repeated violence against his mother. Stewart wrote about his experiences with domestic violence in The Guardian in 2009. The stage, he confessed there, seemed to him "a far safer place" than reality; he saw acting as a way to escape his home life.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

In a recent development, patrick began acting at the age of 12. At 16, he left school early and, thanks to a scholarship, studied acting in Bristol, England. Along the way, he worked as a journalist. In 1965, he became an official member of the Royal Shakespeare Organization, and remained with the theather company from 1966 to 1982. Such was his passion for the great English playwright and lyricist that he even shared his sonnets on his Twitter account during the 2020 coronavirus pandemic.

According to recent reports, stewart dazzled the theater world with his own stage adaptation of Charles Dickens' 1843 tale "A Christmas Carol." He played more than 30 roles himself. After its 1987 premiere in Stewart's hometown of Mirfield, the one-man show became a critics' favorite and a long-running hit on Broadway in Upcoming York.

Sources indicate that in the same year,  Stewart went from being a stage actor to an international TV star. Star Trek producer Robert Justman offered him the role of Captain Jean-Luc Picard, one of the main characters in a new edition of the popular TV series "Star Trek: The Next Generation.".

The successful Shakespearean hesitated. Until then, he had never worked in Hollywood. But his agent encouraged him to accept the role, Stewart recalled in a 2020 interview with the German newspaper Die Welt. "You can accept the offer as a start for now. It won't be a substantial deal, you can't revive a series as iconic as Star Trek anyway.".

But his agent was to be proven wrong: Stewart led the Starship Enterprise through its galactic adventures for seven seasons and four full-length feature films. The TV series had astronomical success on Earth in a very short time. At first, the producers were at odds as to whether Stewart's British accent could really fit the role of commander of a US starship in the 24th century, but it soon became impossible to imagine the series without the subtly diplomatic Captain Picard, who often quoted Shakespeare while at the helm. It seemed as if all the time he had spent as a Shakespearean actor had prepared him to command the Enterprise, Stewart once remarked with a wink. When the cult series ended in 1994, he had ruled out ever returning to the Enterprise's command center.

In 2010, the actor was knighted by the Queen of England. Stewart considered it the greatest honor of his career to stand alongside acting greats such as Sir Laurence Olivier and Sir Alec Guinness.

Beyond the screen, Stewart has long used his voice for social and human rights causes. In recent years, he has drawn attention to concerns such as violence against women, age discrimination and the protection of children.

In a June 2020 interview, "Playboy" asked the Latest York resident whether he was considering retiring from acting. "Never! That would mean giving up my life," replied Stewart, who was approaching his 80th birthday at the time. He was filming the second of three seasons of "Star Trek: Picard." The series ends with a final episode in which the retired Starfleet admiral makes his last appearance. In the series, Picard retires to his family vineyard in France but is drawn back into space to confront new threats to the Federation.

This series also showcases Stewart's affection for his pit bull, Ginger. In "Star Trek: Picard," Picard also has a pit bull, a loyal four-legged companion named Number One — a deliberate reference to Stewart's real-life love of the breed. For his efforts to combat prejudice against pit bulls and to support their adoption, Stewart was honored by the US animal welfare organization ASPCA, among others.

In 2024, he published his memoir "Making it So." In it, he recounts his passion for theater and his love of Shakespeare.

Now, at the age of 86, the British actor has finally departed for another galaxy. Farewell, Patrick Stewart!

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

There will be many more Champions League nights for Rio Ngumoha, although the 18-year-old will always remember this career landmark when his teenage skill plunged the opposition into fearful indecision and decided the game.

Industry observers note that this young man has not yet played 40 senior games but there is no doubting the quality. Alexis Mac Allister scored twice, Liverpool came from two goals behind, and it all ended with a panic that meant they came close to chucking it away again. But what everyone could agree on from this strange match of fluctuating fortunes was that Ngumoha looks like one of the best young players in Europe. He is also a bona fide two-sided winger, winning this game for Liverpool from the right wing rather than his conventional left-wing role.

In a recent development, ngumoha created the second Liverpool goal for Ronald Araújo and then the third for Mac Allister with the game’s best moment. That was an electrifying run into a group of converging yellow shirts in which he beat two men and still retained the composure to pick out Mac Allister in the area. Even as the Argentine ran to the Kop to celebrate, that stand was chanting the name of the teenager from east London. Ngumoha was one of three academy boys in Andoni Iraola’s XI, along with Lewis Koumas and Trey Nyoni, and all had an impact.

Magic from Rio Ngumoha 🤩🪄 Alexis Mac Allister puts Liverpool ahead with his second goal of the night ⚽️ https://t.co/3FTNWOUYhl.

Iraola noted later that Ngumoha had taken care of the defensive work too against Sergi Cardona, an attacking left-back who scored his team’s second goal. From an attacking point of view, Iraola agreed, Ngumoha had periods of the game when he looked unstoppable. “If we can put Rio in situations one-v-one, he makes plays, [and] he produces things,” Iraola remarked. “The assist for Alexis is a lovely play. He could go down for a penalty but he decides to continue which is a great decision. Also endurance-wise he is able to play more minutes.”.

He becomes the youngest Liverpool player in Champions League history to register an assist in the competition. For Iraola it will be hard to leave Ngumoha out of the game against in-form Brighton and Hove Albion on Sunday. “I believe in myself to do it,” Ngumoha remarked to Amazon Prime TV. “The more chances we get, the more it makes the opposition worry. I just keep going and be ruthless.”.

Industry observers note that iraola would later bring on the three £100m attackers whom he had left on the bench, with Sunday’s game in mind. Florian Wirtz, a half-time arrival, scored the fourth and Bradley Barcola and Alexander Isak would later come on. Hard to call how it might go at home to Brighton. Liverpool’s defending was erratic at times, but their comeback was impressive.

The floodgates are opening ⚽️ Florian Wirtz scores his first goal of the season for Liverpool 🇩🇪 https://t.co/5HP72tA3bE.

Iraola made major changes at half-time, substituting Araújo and playing without a conventional right-back for the second half. It was brave and changed the momentum of the game, pushing his team higher up the pitch in what looked like a man-to-man marking arrangement. It enabled Iraola’s players to deny Villarreal the space and possession they had enjoyed in the first half when they had taken a two-goal lead – chiefly because of the mistakes of the home team. However much that was destabilising for Liverpool, by half-time they were level.

Recent findings suggest that “They are so good on the ball,” Iraola said of Villarreal afterwards. Indeed, Villarreal’s manager Iñigo Pérez, a former Athletic team-mate of the Liverpool manager, was a coach whom Iraola sought to appoint at Bournemouth. “People probably don’t rate them [Villarreal],” Iraola said, “but after Barça they are probably the best in La Liga. They have 61 per cent of possession. Probably they have not had the results they deserve. If you are not really aggressive, you are not going to get the ball.

“We didn’t take as much risk. We were struggling because it is not a team that you can just press a bit. Either you go all the way or you will struggle without the ball.” Once Liverpool had done so, he mentioned, his team had “won a lot of duels”. He was right in that respect. With the space squeezed, it was the power of Liverpool’s midfield that was telling.

Virgil van Dijk gave the first goal to Villarreal’s small No 9 Georges Mikautadze who had looked up to that point like he was hopelessly mismatched against the Liverpool captain and Jérémy Jacquet. Van Dijk’s misjudged header back to Alisson let in the striker, who did well to gather the ball and then hit it early. Cody Gakpo, Dominik Szoboszlai and Isak returned from injury to strengthen Liverpool at Brentford, although Szoboszlai has been lost for a few weeks following another hamstring complication.

Villarreal have punched well above their weight in Europe for the past few decades, reaching two European Cup semi-finals (beaten by Arsenal in 2006 as well as Liverpool in 2022) and winning the Europa League under Unai Emery in 2021.

It has been revealed that they have been mediocre in La Liga so far this season though, 12th after nine games on nine points and with a goal difference of zero. Villarreal’s best player is probably Senegalese central midfielder Pape Gueye, and former Arsenal winger Nicolas Pépé is also in their ranks. 📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Undergraduate students on university campuses played a significant part in spreading viral variants during the COVID-19 pandemic.Credit: Leonard Ortiz/Digital First Media/Orange County Register/Getty.

Universities have become hotbeds of SARS-CoV-2 transmission, according to a massive analysis of more than 85,000 viral genome sequences and other data collected from people with COVID-19.

COVID can wake up a slew of dormant viruses inside you.

COVID can wake up a slew of dormant viruses inside you.

Sources indicate that the study, published on 19 November in the journal Cell1, finds that viral transmission between 2021 and 2023 was highest in adolescents aged 15–18 in schools, undergraduates at university and residents in nursing facilities. Undergraduates, in particular, were consistently the first group to start spreading emerging genetic variants of SARS-CoV-2.

Recent findings suggest that surprisingly, however, staff members at all three types of institution had about the same risk of contracting COVID-19 as did those in their surrounding communities. So, for example, professors were about as likely to get COVID-19 from the coffee baristas in their university towns as they were to get it from a student at their university.

The analysis is among the largest to bring together viral genomic sequences and medical data from people with COVID-19. “The scale is truly impressive,” indicates Bill Hanage, who studies the evolution of infectious diseases at the Harvard T.H. Chan School of Public Health in Boston, Massachusetts. “It’s an example of the depth and the detail of the picture that can be painted using the medium of population genomics.”.

The findings were based on data collected from COVID-19 tests taken by people in Massachusetts between November 2021 and January 2023. The genomic data allowed researchers to trace the path of SARS-CoV-2 variants that emerged over time, and to link this with epidemiological data about the study participants, such as their age and whether they had been vaccinated against COVID-19.

COVID jabs for kids: they’re safe and they work — so why is uptake so patchy?

COVID jabs for kids: they’re safe and they work — so why is uptake so patchy?

Sources indicate that overall, the team found that booster vaccinations helped to reduce SARS-CoV-2 transmission. This was true even for BA.1, an Omicron variant that started to circulate in Massachusetts in late 2021 — a striking result because COVID-19 vaccines at that time hadn’t yet been updated to protect against BA.1, Hanage notes. “That’s an important illustration of how vaccines, even when they’re not perfect, can still be beneficial,” he says.

Tottenham Hotspur have been handed a potential latest concern over James Maddison's fitness ahead of Sunday's Premier League clash with Sunderland.

The Lilywhites hit the road to face the Black Cats at the Stadium of Light this Sunday, aiming to register their fifth win from their last six Premier League matches.

Spurs' recent resurgence has propelled them into the top half of the Premier League table, as they bounced back from their 1-0 defeat at Leeds United by dispatching Ipswich Town 2-0 on home soil.

Roberto De Zerbi's men got the better of the Tractor Boys despite the absence of Sandro Tonali, who was a last-minute omission from the matchday squad due to illness.

The Italian was filmed being put through his paces with the team in Tuesday's open training session, though, handing Spurs a welcome boost ahead of their trek north.

However, according to Sky Sports News journalist Michael Bridge, Maddison was restricted to indoor work, raising fears of another potential fitness concern for the playmaker.

Sandro Tonali back after missing the win over Ipswich. James Maddison doing indoor work. #THFC https://t.co/EsvY9oqNqb.

Maddison has only made three Premier League starts this season, having spent the majority of the 2025-26 campaign recovering from a serious ACL concern before also picking up a shoulder problem.

The 30-year-old was an unused substitute against Crystal Palace and Leeds earlier this month, and he was taken off in the 64th minute of Saturday's victory over Ipswich.

It is not clear whether Maddison's absence from team training was down to a genuine new injury for the Englishman, or if he is simply being protected ahead of the weekend's fixture.

Nevertheless, for a player who has already missed 73 games for club and country since joining Tottenham from Leicester City in 2023, any minor fitness development could set off alarm bells in Spurs fans' heads.

While Maddison's situation will be closely monitored, Tonali's return from illness is one of two early boosts that Tottenham have received for the trip to Sunderland.

The Black Cats will be unable to call on Kevin Danso this weekend, as the on-loan Tottenham defender is ineligible to face his parent club.

Danso's absence may not have a massive bearing on Regis Le Bris's selection, though, as the Austrian has been an unused substitute in each of Sunderland's last three Premier League games.

Danso started each of the Black Cats' first five top-flight matches of the newly introduced season, but he has not played a minute of Premier League football since being sent off against Bournemouth on October 18.

Breaking: The Women's World Cup is coming home... but 2035 cannot be treated as a fix for the game's problems, writes TARA ANSON-WALSH

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (840 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dailymail

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Published: 14:36 EST, 23 November 2026 | Updated: 17:04 EST, 23 November 2026.
  • The United Kingdom will host the 2035 Women's World Cup, the first football World Cup to be staged on these shores since 1966, it was declared to much fanfare on Monday.
  • Yet while the countdown can now officially begin, the biggest challenges facing the women's game cannot be kicked eight-and-a-half years down the road.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

By TARA ANSON-WALSH, FOOTBALL REPORTER.

Published: 14:36 EST, 23 November 2026 | Updated: 17:04 EST, 23 November 2026.

The United Kingdom will host the 2035 Women's World Cup, the first football World Cup to be staged on these shores since 1966, it was declared to much fanfare on Monday.

Yet while the countdown can now officially begin, the biggest challenges facing the women's game cannot be kicked eight-and-a-half years down the road.

Over in Zurich, FIFA president Gianni Infantino undertook his usual long-winded and self-serving monologue which precedes these ceremonies, in which he heralded the 'incredible growth' of the Women's World Cup, describing a time when they 'didn't exist'.

'We all remember the last Women's World Cup,' the embattled 56-year-old Italian mentioned, calling it 'a huge success'.

The irony, of course, is that the last Women's World Cup in Australia and New Zealand is remembered by many for all the wrong reasons, with newspaper back pages peppered with images of Spain captain Jenni Hermoso's kiss with the former president of Spain's FA, Luis Rubiales, for days after the final.

Rubiales was later convicted of sexual assault for the incident, which triggered widespread protests across the country and overshadowed Spain's terrific 1-0 triumph over England in Sydney.

Gianni Infantino undertook his usual long-winded and self-serving monologue which precedes these ceremonies, in which he heralded the 'incredible growth' of the Women's World Cup.

Rubiales was later convicted of sexual assault for the incident, which triggered widespread protests across the country and overshadowed Spain's terrific 1-0 triumph over England.

There is an added layer of irony in that Infantino had, two days before the 2023 final, angered many women worldwide with yet another controversial speech in which he told them: 'You have the power to change', but that they had to 'convince us men what we have to do'.

Alongside this patronising statement, Infantino also insisted that equal pay at the World Cup 'would not solve anything'.

Three years later, Infantino is unfortunately still at the helm, while UEFA's attempts to unseat him following his controversial bid to sell off the World Cup now look to have failed spectacularly, with the football despot increasingly likely to secure a fourth term.

Industry observers note that what the social and political landscape will look like by the time this women's footballing bonanza arrives on these shores in 2035 remains unclear. What is clear, however, is that the game's continued progress will require more than the record attendances and soaring commercial revenues the FA are predicting.

It will require the figures who have too often held it back to finally step aside, and that process should begin with the likes of Infantino being shown the door.

Sources indicate that it will require those at the top of English football to put their heads together and work out how to stem falling attendances in the league. The average attendance across the first eight WSL matchweeks of 2024-25 was 8,173. Last season it was 7,472. This season, it is tracking at around 5,677.

And third, it will require somewhere other than Wembley to stage the final.

Wembley was, of course, the scene of Chloe Kelly's moment of madness, yet by the time the 2035 Women's World Cup comes around it will also have hosted the men's finals of Euro 2024 and 2028.

The FA paid off its debt on the national stadium in 2024, 17 years after its reopening, and is no longer obligated to host major events there to service repayments.

The rules have been left open for another venue to emerge to host the final, such as Man United's proposed new 100,000 stadium.

While under current FIFA regulations, Wembley is the only one of the proposed 22 stadiums that meets the requirements to host a final, the rules have been left open enough for another venue to emerge should a suitable stadium be completed before 2035.

Step up Sir Jim Ratcliffe, although please refer back to point one in this regard – the Manchester United co-owner who famously asked former captain Katie Zelem 'what do you do here?' while touring the club's women's facilities.

United's proposed new 100,000-seater stadium was included in the 2035 bid and could yet come under consideration from FIFA.

While there are still many hurdles to clear before then, hosting a tournament final in Manchester would undoubtedly be huge for the women's game, not least given the optics of a bid built around being 'all together', described as 'a rallying cry to unite people through football'.

London should not be the epicentre of the tournament, not if the intention is to spread the women's game across the United Kingdom rather than concentrate it in the capital, where Arsenal's attendances continue to dwarf those of every other WSL club.

In other words, the women's game in this country cannot be put on hold until 2035.

Industry observers note that it cannot afford to wait eight-and-a-half years for this World Cup to come and rescue it. Time to get cracking.

#94793. Industry News: The dachshund, a humorous icon with political symbolism

📅 30 Oct 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1182 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Dw ↗ Open Full Page

Industry News: The dachshund, a humorous icon with political symbolism

📅 30 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1182 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dw

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that pablo Picasso was renowned for having numerous muses — mostly women with whom he also had harmful relationships.
  • Before becoming his most famous canine model, Lump originally belonged to US photojournalist David Douglas Duncan.
  • The dog and the photographer visited Picasso at his villa in Cannes in 1967.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that pablo Picasso was renowned for having numerous muses — mostly women with whom he also had harmful relationships. But there's at least one of these muses who was freed from toxic romantic entanglement: a cute dachshund called Lump.

Before becoming his most famous canine model, Lump originally belonged to US photojournalist David Douglas Duncan.

The dog and the photographer visited Picasso at his villa in Cannes in 1967. According to Duncan, upon their first encounter, Lump jumped right onto Picasso's lap. He apparently "decided" to stay with the painter, and they lived together for six years.

The story does not reveal how Lump's decision was communicated, but that immediate special bound was immortalized through art: Picasso painted the dachshund's portrait directly onto a ceramic dinner plate that day, and Duncan did a series of photos documenting them together while the work was created.

It has been revealed that the plate and the photos are on show at the latest exhibition "The Dachshund. An Icon off the Leash" held at the Kunsthalle Bremen until March 28, 2027.

Lump also appears in many of Picasso's series of paintings reinterpreting Diego Velazquez's masterwork "Las Meninas," in which the original work's large mastiff was replaced with Picasso's adoptive pet.

With their long ears and extreme length compared to their short legs, dachshunds have a silhouette that's instantly recognizable: "It's really a dog with an iconic shape, and that makes them interesting for many things" — from art to advertisement, says exhibition curator and art historian Annett Reckert.

It has been revealed that alongside Picasso, a surprising number of crucial artists, including Andy Warhol, Otto Dix, David Hockney, Max Liebermann and Rosemarie Trockel, have paid tribute to the dachshund. "It's striking how often the dachshund has served as a muse, model and studio accomplice for them," Reckert tells DW.

Combined with this prolific artistic career, the dachshund can equally be explored from a historical perspective, since "there's also the fact that we associate them with something German," the curator adds.

According to recent reports, bred to track and chase badgers, foxes, rabbits and other burrowing animals, the dachshund originated in Germany over 300 years ago. Breed standards were established in 1879, and the German Teckel Club (DTK) — one of the oldest dog breeding organizations in Germany — was founded in 1888.

The name combines the German words "Dachs" (badger) and "Hund" (dog), literally translating to "badger dog." But Germans more commonly call them Dackel or Teckel.

Because of their long, narrow build, dachshunds are also colloquially known in English-speaking countries as wiener dogs or sausage dogs.

Beyond their role as hunting dogs, dachshunds have a surprisingly rich place in German cultural history, from bourgeois stereotype to Olympic icon.

Germany's last emperor, Kaiser Wilhelm II, was an avid dachshund enthusiast and owned several of them.

Industry observers note that two of his dogs, Wadl and Hexlsome, made history by causing a minor diplomatic incident during a visit to the estate of Archduke Franz Ferdinand, Konopiste Castle, in 1908. The dachshunds reportedly killed one of the archduke's prized golden pheasants. The attack was widely commented on in aristocratic circles, and Kaiser Wilhelm II was forced to issue a formal apology.

The pheasant incident was obviously not as consequential as another event involving Franz Ferdinand, heir to the Austro-Hungarian throne: his assassination in Sarajevo on June 28, 1914, which became the primary catalyst of World War I.

In a recent development, still, the dachshund remained present throughout this global conflict. In propaganda maps and political cartoons, Germany was represented as a dachshund, the British as a bulldog and the French, a poodle.

The popularity of the dachshund in the United States plummeted during the World War I because of this association; those who owned one called their dogs "liberty hounds" instead of using the German word.

During World War II, dachshunds were used for military tasks such as mine detection.

However, their missions weren't as outlandish as the stories published by the UK's tabloid press relatively recently, which claimed that the Nazis aimed to build armies of talking dachshunds. The rumors followed the publication of a non-fiction book on dogs published in 2011, "Amazing Dogs: A Cabinet of Canine Curiosities," which outlined Nazi research into dogs' — including dachshunds' — intelligence and personalities.

Industry observers note that the dachshund definitely didn't fit into the Nazis' aesthetics: "They were used in the war, too, but not in the same way as other dogs. After all, they weren't the kind of dog a Nazi would have wanted to be seen with for the sake of appearances," notes Reckert. "Take Hitler, for instance: He famously made public appearances with his German Shepherd, Blondie. They would rather be seen with a Doberman or dogs that looked big and dangerous.".

The endearing potential of the dachshund is actually one of the ideas that guided Reckert in her curation of the exhibition. They "simply give the impression that they have a sense of humor," the art historian says. "That's an attribution, of course. But they really do spread good cheer and have a truly likable character.".

In the 1970s, this slightly absurd and cheerful domestic companion inspired a figure embodying a latest image for West Germany: the official mascot for the 1972 Summer Olympics in Munich, Waldi.

A stark contrast to the heavy symbols that represented Germany during the Third Reich — the eagle, Germania, forests, Wagner and Prussian discipline — the mascot created by renowned graphic designer Otl Aicher and his intern, Elena Schwaiger, was as iconic as the shape of the dachshund.

The designer was vehemently against including brown or any of Germany's national colors — red, black and gold — in the brand identity. Instead, he went for delicate pastel shades: "The approach to color was truly visionary," notes Reckert. "Their intention was something we are still working on today — something we still haven't completely achieved: an open, cheerful, democratic and colorful Germany.".

It has been revealed that still today, right-wing extremist groups attempt to co-opt the dachshund as a subtle nationalist fashion symbol that appears on ties or socks, inspired by accessories worn by Alexander Gauland. On the other hand, "Dachshunds Against the Right" has also emerged as a counter-protest movement.

But altogether, Reckert has focused on the dachshund as a symbol of friendliness and joy while conceiving "The Dachshund. An Icon off the Leash." The exhibition includes halls that are open to small dogs and even features artworks and performances specifically designed for them.

Sources indicate that the feedback Reckert's been getting in the run-up to the show also aligns with this cheerful image. She notes that hardly a day goes by without something arriving in the mail related to the dachshund — whether pictures, artworks or information about dachshund-related events.

Industry observers note that "It's really crazy," she states, showing examples of the stuff she's received. "I've never had an exhibition that was greeted ahead of its opening in such a friendly, diverse way. It's almost a bit uncanny, really.".

The visitors will bring a four-game unbeaten run in all competitions into this match, but Crete will enter the European fixture off the back of a 2-0 loss to Panathinaikos in the Greek Super League.

OFI have a record of two wins and two losses from their four matches in the league stage of this season's Europa League, with six points leaving them in 16th position in the overall table.

The Club started their league phase with a 2-0 win over Hoffenheim before losing back-to-back games in the competition against Rennes and Bayer Leverkusen.

However, Christos Kontis' side posted a 2-0 victory over H. Beer Sheva in their last Europa League game on November 5, so they will be aiming to make it back-to-back wins in the tournament.

OFI are playing in the league stage/group stage of a major European tournament for the first time since the 1995-96 campaign, and this is also the first time that they have ever qualified for this round of the UEFA Cup/Europa League.

The Club have European matches to come against Benfica, Sturm Graz and Lech before the end of the group stage in early 2027.

Anderlecht, meanwhile, have also won two and lost two of their four matches in this season's Europa League league stage, with six points leaving them 15th in the table.

The Belgian club started their league phase with a 2-1 loss to Lyon, before going down 1-0 to Dinamo Zagreb in the middle of October, but they have won their last two matches in the tournament against Jagiellonia and Red Bull Salzburg to move onto six points.

Vitor Bruno's side will enter this match off the back of a 1-0 win over Leuven in the league, with the result leaving them in fifth position in Belgium's top flight.

Anderlecht will face Hoffenheim, Sunderland and Marseille in their three European matches after this one, and it would be a surprise if they were not present in the knockout round.

The Purple and Whites won this competition back in 1982-83, and this is their first Europa League league phase campaign since 2024-25.

“Annoyed” Kevin De Bruyne faces uncertain Napoli future ahead of Man City return

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

By Oliver Thomas | 24 Nov 2026 13:05.

Manchester City legend Kevin De Bruyne is preparing for an emotional homecoming at the Etihad Stadium on Tuesday night, though his current spell with Napoli has been clouded by transfer speculation and internal friction.

After winning 19 trophies during a glittering 10-year career at Man City, the 35-year-old playmaker reluctantly left the club at the end of the 2024-25 season when the decision was made to not extend his contract.

De Bruyne subsequently signed for Napoli as a free agent, embarking on a fresh challenge in Italian football, but his debut campaign was struck by injury, starting only 16 matches across all competitions as Napoli surrendered their Serie A crown to Inter Milan.

The Belgium international has since played in all 16 games for Napoli across Serie A and the Champions League this term, chipping in with four goals and two assists while operating in a deeper midfield position under head coach Massimiliano Allegri.

De Bruyne is part of an aging Napoli side that are at the moment languishing down in eighth place in Serie A and sit 27th in the Champions League standings after losing three of their opening four League Phase games.

Tensions boiled over during Napoli’s heavy 4-1 UCL loss at Porto earlier this month, where teammates had to separate De Bruyne and striker Lorenzo Lucca following an angry on-pitch row.

"Speaking about the pitch, De Bruyne is the best player this year at Napoli. The point is that the whole team is having difficulties, Naples-based journalist Vincenzo Credendino told BBC Sport.

"We saw that there is a problem, at least between De Bruyne and Lorenzo Lucca. Their acting was very, very clear and I think that in that time, the two of them were wrong.

"On one hand you cannot swear at another team-mate but on the other hand, De Bruyne reproached Lucca without encouraging him, so it was a bad show.".

As De Bruyne enters the twilight years of his career, it has been suggested that the “spark never really ignited” between the midfielder and the Naples outfit, raising uncertainty over his future at the club.

When asked about his future at a press conference ahead of Napoli’s Champions League clash with Man City, De Bruyne said: "Not a lot I can say for the moment. I have played at 100% until now and obviously I am not 20 years old, I am turning 36.

Sources indicate that "There is a lot of things going in my mind but there is not a lot to say. I am playing good football, trying to help the team to do well and it has been a bit of a challenging season with a lot of things happening.".

De Bruyne will soon be entering the final six months of his Napoli contract and will be free to negotiate pre-contract agreements with foreign clubs in January.

De Bruyne has also expressed his annoyance over the backlash he and his family have received following controversial comments made by the player’s wife in September.

His wife Michele reportedly told Belgian magazine NINA about their desire to move back to Belgium, saying "the sooner we get there, the better" as De Bruyne leads a "very restricted life" in Naples.

Addressing the media fallout, De Bruyne replied: "To be honest, I am pretty annoyed because if you read the article, that none of you have read, to understand what she noted.

Recent findings suggest that "I was away in Belgium and a lot of noise came and a lot of bad reactions to my wife and family. I saw pictures of my house, I don't think it is OK but it is what it is and some press created this in Italy. I don't know why.

"Nobody knows my life, you will never know. People who work with me are not allowed to say anything but obviously it is something that I take away and think about. It has not been nice for my wife or for my family.".

De Bruyne has since been linked with a sensational Premier League return in January, while Dutch giants PSV Eindhoven are understood to have failed with a €2m (£1.7m) opening offer to sign him in the Latest Year, with Napoli valuing the midfielder closer to €8m (£6.7m), according to Credendino.

Napoli boss Allegri has interestingly refused to rule out a mid-season departure for De Bruyne, stating on Monday that transfer decisions are "down to the players and who wants to leave" once January arrives.

Meanwhile, De Bruyne has spoken out for the first time since Man City were found guilty of breaching Premier League financial regulations.

Breaking: Embarrassing name? How we live with names we don't like

📅 23 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1045 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dw

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • As a child growing up in Australia, Louise Pain hated her surname.
  • "People used to tease me; I was called things like 'Pain in the a*s,'" she told DW.
  • The jokes have followed her throughout her life, even after she moved to Germany.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

As a child growing up in Australia, Louise Pain hated her surname.

"People used to tease me; I was called things like 'Pain in the a*s,'" she told DW. "I remember actively hating my surname when I was a child and wanting to change it.".

The jokes have followed her throughout her life, even after she moved to Germany. But one thing did eventually change: Pain's feelings about her own name.

Recent findings suggest that names are not only a fundamental part of how we identify ourselves — they can, beyond teasing, also influence how other people treat us. So, what happens if we dislike our own name, or if it is perceived negatively by those around us?

Industry observers note that "A person's name is vital to their sense of identity," psychoanalyst Mikita Brottman told DW. "When someone has an embarrassing name, that embarrassment can be incorporated into their identity.".

Research on name bias has linked negatively perceived names with romantic rejection,as well as lower educational outcomes, lower self-esteem and more frequent smoking.

This suggests that names could influence our life trajectory, namely through self-esteem and opportunity.

Industry observers note that but a person's relationship with their name is not necessarily fixed. Pain's lived experience, and that of another woman with the first name Tiny, indicates how people can find ways to reclaim, and even come to value, names that once triggered ridicule and rejection.

Names can act as "signals" when you first meet someone, personality psychologist Jochen Gebauer told DW. Those signals may lose importance as people get to know each other, but Gebauer noted their effects could also accumulate over a lifetime, potentially contributing to "real measurable advantages and disadvantages.".

In a recent development, research led by sociologist Anthony Lee found that a name can evoke inaccurate assumptions about intelligence, competence, trustworthiness, sociability and attractiveness. For Pain, other people's reactions have extended beyond jokes. In high school, a teacher refused to believe that 'Pain' was her real surname and reprimanded her in front of the class.

"Your name couldn't possibly be Pain. Write your real name!" she recalled the teacher saying.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

In Lee's UK-based research, less familiar names tended to fall along a dimension partly characterized as "weirdness," which may help explain why difficult-to-pronounce or culturally unfamiliar names receive more negative evaluations.

Tiny, now 54, encountered the same questions about her unfamiliar name growing up in Greece.

Her parents had adapted "Tiny" to "Tinie" to make it sound more Greek, but people would repeatedly ask what her real or baptismal name was.

Even relatives have refused to accept it. Recently, two elderly aunts introduced her to someone as "Haritini," a conventional Greek name.

"I didn't even bother correcting them at this point," Tiny told DW.

Tiny's relationship with her name has also evolved.

"The jokes [from others] got repetitive and boring pretty fast, so at least I was left with the sense that I have something unique with my name going on.".

It has been revealed that pain, now 40, discovered how much cultural context could change the reaction to her surname when she began learning her father's native French as a teenager. In French, 'pain' means bread.

"People started calling me 'Bread! Louise Bread.'".

Later, after moving to Germany, the jokes became mostly bread-related rather than the more scathing ones she had experienced in Australia. "That helped me to feel better about my name," she remarked.

As they got older, both Pain and Tiny developed coping strategies to pre-empt people's reactions to their names.

In a recent development, tiny sometimes introduces herself with: "Hi, I'm Tiny. It's my name and not a statement," or, "I'm Tiny. Not a difficult name to live up to.".

"This usually stops people from asking awkward questions.".

Pain also began to embrace the humor surrounding her name.

"I was convinced that I should become either a doctor or a dominatrix, or perhaps both, to become either 'Doctor Pain,' or 'Mistress Pain.'".

"Names can conjure that whole spectrum of shame and pride," psychoanalyst Melissa Daum told DW.

Pain now finds that people tend to see her surname as "funny and endearing… it's become something that is more of a funny talking point.".

But the childhood discomfort has not entirely disappeared. When Pain thinks about having children, her feelings about the name become more complicated.

Industry observers note that "I don't really want to pass on my surname ... so there is a deeper wound there.".

But Pain also believes her father would be deeply hurt if future children had a different name. The surname she once hated connects her to him and to her French heritage.

"Something that once feels like an inconvenience or a source of self-consciousness can become a marker of distinctiveness, history, or belonging," Daum said.

Tiny describes a similar ambivalence.

"My parents seemingly made an unfortunate choice, but by now I have embraced both the name and the sense of uniqueness that comes with it.".

That does not mean she uses Tiny everywhere. She avoids it on dating apps because "Tiny might give off the wrong message," and does not use it in her email address when she wants to appear professional.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

Pain, meanwhile, uses a Germanized version of the French word for bread as her social media surname.

Online, people have more control over what name they present to others. As Daum put it: "Choosing one's own name can feel like an act of mastery, even a refusal of that original passivity: I will decide what I am called and how I am encountered.".

But accepting a name does not necessarily mean embracing it in every situation.

Sources indicate that pain once wanted to change her surname. Tiny considered using her middle name in her thirties. Neither ultimately abandoned the names that had caused them difficulties.

For Tiny, at least, a name that once made her feel awkward has become something she can imagine carrying for the rest of her life.

"It might be cute to eventually be a granny called Tiny.".

Jack Grealish returned to the Everton squad for the first time since being made unavailable for selection due to a breach of club discipline, and came off the bench at half-time against Brentford on Monday.

In a recent development, the Manchester City loanee was punished by the club for failing to report to training sessions and missed several matches. He had not featured for four games: one because of illness, then a 'breach of club discipline' and a lack of fitness thereafter.

'We will get on with things. The team is going really well at the moment and what I don't want to do is turn it into a Jack story because it shouldn't be.'.

Recent findings suggest that pushed if that suggests he will not play on Monday night, Moyes replied: 'He could easily. He is back in the squad, he is a good player. Who knows?'.

Jack Grealish (right) returned to Everton action on Monday for the first time since being punished for missing training.

He was named on the bench against Brentford, coming on for Tyrique George at half-time.

According to recent reports, everton had won their last three games and went into Monday's match sixth in the table. The result, though, was a blow as they dropped to ninth.

Recent findings suggest that asked what Grealish can offer, Moyes added: 'Jack can offer us a lot. I want more from him, I want him to show more than he has done. I want him to give me more assists, goals.

Recent findings suggest that 'But there's lots of things about him which we need and he's good at retaining the ball, giving us good possession, carrying. So we hope that he can get back to those levels and give us what we need.

'I think this time last year he was probably sitting on five or six assists so we're hoping to get that.'.

Grealish's social media apology came after he featured in a behind-closed-doors match during the international break.

'Nice to be back out there with the boys today after a few good days training!' Grealish wrote. 'I want to apologise to the fans (and) everyone at the club for not being able to help the team the last few weeks.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Liverpool aren't in the best run of form at the moment.

The Reds are miles away from first-placed Arsenal and, right now, it doesn't feel like they have the quality among their ranks to get back to the top of the Premier League table.

Fans expected Liverpool to be challenging for the title this season, especially after their £150 million + spend in the summer.

That obviously hasn't worked out with fans now questioning whether the club even has enough strength among their ranks to get them where they need to be.

Right now, the January transfer window is just over a month away and, fans are expecting a lot of change to take place.

So, the fact that one of their reported targets are '100%' on their way out of Anfield is a very good sign.

Barcelona are '100%' going to sell Alejandro Balde in January.

Since the arrival of Ronald Araujo, Liverpool's defence has been fairly solid.

The Uruguayan has brought an extra layer of stability to Andoni Iraola's ranks and has helped take a lot of pressure off the shoulders of Jeremy Jacquet.

Thanks to how strong Araujo has been, Jacquet has been allowed to take his time to settle into Premier League life and, he's probably been one of Liverpool's best signings thanks to that.

Right now, it's unclear what the Reds' priorities are going to be in January but, thanks to an upgrade from journalist Juan Jesus, a bit of a better insight has now been given to fans.

Industry observers note that "Despite Deco’s words, Alejandro Balde is 100% out. Several clubs know this and are closely monitoring his situation, including Manchester United, PSG, AC Milan and Liverpool," he shared via X.

"Barça expects the bidding to drive up the price and is confident of securing his departure for at least 45–50 million euros.".

Alejandro Balde's newly introduced price tag is expensive.

When talk of Liverpool being linked with Balde first emerged, the deal was pitched as an unmissable offer for the Reds.

Talk of a deal worth around £30 million was being mooted with other clubs such as Manchester United also linked with an interest.

However, the fact that the deal could end up costing around €50 million (£41.9 million) makes things a little harder to understand.

Obviously, Balde is an incredible player and would help solve two of the Reds' main concerns going into 2027.

But, £41.9 million is a lot of money for the club to spend on another left-back.

Everyone thought that Milos Kerkez was going to be the second coming of Andy Robertson after he was signed for £40 million but, in reality, he still needs to do a lot of work to improve his game.

Right now, it's unclear what plans Liverpool have for the upcoming transfer window but, if they don't make a couple of meaningful signings, by the end of the 2026-27 season, they'll be fighting for a Champions League place, rather than the title.
